soc2.name: AICPA Trust Services Criteria (SOC 2)
soc2.official_citation: TSP Section 100 — 2017 Trust Services Criteria for Security, Availability, Processing Integrity, Confidentiality, and Privacy (With Revised Points of Focus — 2022)
soc2.scope: Service organization controls audit framework. Common criteria CC1-CC5 align to the 17 COSO Internal Control — Integrated Framework principles. Common criteria CC6-CC9 are supplemental criteria for logical/physical access, system operations, change management, and risk mitigation. Category-specific criteria for Availability (A series), Processing Integrity (PI series), Confidentiality (C series), and Privacy (P series) supplement the common criteria.
soc2.source: AICPA — TSP Section 100, distributed at https://www.aicpa-cima.com/resources/download/2017-trust-services-criteria-with-revised-points-of-focus-2022 (registration-gated public download).
soc2.verified_against: Local PDF of TSP Section 100 (cover page identifies it as the AICPA-published 2017 Trust Services Criteria with Revised Points of Focus — 2022). All sub-criterion titles below were verbatim-extracted from pages 14-50 of that document on 2026-05-10.

common_criteria_subcriteria.CC1.1: COSO Principle 1: The entity demonstrates a commitment to integrity and ethical values.
common_criteria_subcriteria.CC1.2: COSO Principle 2: The board of directors demonstrates independence from management and exercises oversight of the development and performance of internal control.
common_criteria_subcriteria.CC1.3: COSO Principle 3: Management establishes, with board oversight, structures, reporting lines, and appropriate authorities and responsibilities in the pursuit of objectives.
common_criteria_subcriteria.CC1.4: COSO Principle 4: The entity demonstrates a commitment to attract, develop, and retain competent individuals in alignment with objectives.
common_criteria_subcriteria.CC1.5: COSO Principle 5: The entity holds individuals accountable for their internal control responsibilities in the pursuit of objectives.
common_criteria_subcriteria.CC2.1: COSO Principle 13: The entity obtains or generates and uses relevant, quality information to support the functioning of internal control.
common_criteria_subcriteria.CC2.2: COSO Principle 14: The entity internally communicates information, including objectives and responsibilities for internal control, necessary to support the functioning of internal control.
common_criteria_subcriteria.CC2.3: COSO Principle 15: The entity communicates with external parties regarding matters affecting the functioning of internal control.
common_criteria_subcriteria.CC3.1: COSO Principle 6: The entity specifies objectives with sufficient clarity to enable the identification and assessment of risks relating to objectives.
common_criteria_subcriteria.CC3.2: COSO Principle 7: The entity identifies risks to the achievement of its objectives across the entity and analyzes risks as a basis for determining how the risks should be managed.
common_criteria_subcriteria.CC3.3: COSO Principle 8: The entity considers the potential for fraud in assessing risks to the achievement of objectives.
common_criteria_subcriteria.CC3.4: COSO Principle 9: The entity identifies and assesses changes that could significantly impact the system of internal control.
common_criteria_subcriteria.CC4.1: COSO Principle 16: The entity selects, develops, and performs ongoing and/or separate evaluations to ascertain whether the components of internal control are present and functioning.
common_criteria_subcriteria.CC4.2: COSO Principle 17: The entity evaluates and communicates internal control deficiencies in a timely manner to those parties responsible for taking corrective action, including senior management and the board of directors, as appropriate.
common_criteria_subcriteria.CC5.1: COSO Principle 10: The entity selects and develops control activities that contribute to the mitigation of risks to the achievement of objectives to acceptable levels.
common_criteria_subcriteria.CC5.2: COSO Principle 11: The entity also selects and develops general control activities over technology to support the achievement of objectives.
common_criteria_subcriteria.CC5.3: COSO Principle 12: The entity deploys control activities through policies that establish what is expected and in procedures that put policies into action.
common_criteria_subcriteria.CC6.1: The entity implements logical access security software, infrastructure, and architectures over protected information assets to protect them from security events to meet the entity's objectives.
common_criteria_subcriteria.CC6.2: Prior to issuing system credentials and granting system access, the entity registers and authorizes new internal and external users whose access is administered by the entity. For those users whose access is administered by the entity, user system credentials are removed when user access is no longer authorized.
common_criteria_subcriteria.CC6.3: The entity authorizes, modifies, or removes access to data, software, functions, and other protected information assets based on roles, responsibilities, or the system design and changes, giving consideration to the concepts of least privilege and segregation of duties, to meet the entity's objectives.
common_criteria_subcriteria.CC6.4: The entity restricts physical access to facilities and protected information assets (for example, data center facilities, backup media storage, and other sensitive locations) to authorized personnel to meet the entity's objectives.
common_criteria_subcriteria.CC6.5: The entity discontinues logical and physical protections over physical assets only after the ability to read or recover data and software from those assets has been diminished and is no longer required to meet the entity's objectives.
common_criteria_subcriteria.CC6.6: The entity implements logical access security measures to protect against threats from sources outside its system boundaries.
common_criteria_subcriteria.CC6.7: The entity restricts the transmission, movement, and removal of information to authorized internal and external users and processes, and protects it during transmission, movement, or removal to meet the entity's objectives.
common_criteria_subcriteria.CC6.8: The entity implements controls to prevent or detect and act upon the introduction of unauthorized or malicious software to meet the entity's objectives.
common_criteria_subcriteria.CC7.1: To meet its objectives, the entity uses detection and monitoring procedures to identify (1) changes to configurations that result in the introduction of new vulnerabilities, and (2) susceptibilities to newly discovered vulnerabilities.
common_criteria_subcriteria.CC7.2: The entity monitors system components and the operation of those components for anomalies that are indicative of malicious acts, natural disasters, and errors affecting the entity's ability to meet its objectives; anomalies are analyzed to determine whether they represent security events.
common_criteria_subcriteria.CC7.3: The entity evaluates security events to determine whether they could or have resulted in a failure of the entity to meet its objectives (security incidents) and, if so, takes actions to prevent or address such failures.
common_criteria_subcriteria.CC7.4: The entity responds to identified security incidents by executing a defined incident-response program to understand, contain, remediate, and communicate security incidents, as appropriate.
common_criteria_subcriteria.CC7.5: The entity identifies, develops, and implements activities to recover from identified security incidents.
common_criteria_subcriteria.CC8.1: The entity authorizes, designs, develops or acquires, configures, documents, tests, approves, and implements changes to infrastructure, data, software, and procedures to meet its objectives.
common_criteria_subcriteria.CC9.1: The entity identifies, selects, and develops risk mitigation activities for risks arising from potential business disruptions.
common_criteria_subcriteria.CC9.2: The entity assesses and manages risks associated with vendors and business partners.

aiuc_1_q3_2026.name: AIUC-1 — AI agent security certification standard
aiuc_1_q3_2026.scope: Certification standard for AI agents. AIUC-1 has 50 requirements that are either mandatory or optional; the applicable set is fixed per agent in a Statement of Applicability signed off by the auditor. All mandatory requirements and core controls apply by default, a mandatory requirement can only be excluded with a documented, legitimate business reason signed off by the auditor, and organizations may add optional requirements and supplemental controls to scope. Certification is granted by an accredited third-party auditor. The standard is revised quarterly.
aiuc_1_q3_2026.source: https://www.aiuc-1.com/scoping (scoping and Statement of Applicability), https://www.aiuc-1.com/evidence (requirement and control catalog), https://www.aiuc-1.com/research/2026-q3-standard-update (Q3-2026 update)

controls.rationale: Risk assessment must identify the individuals who provided the information for the assessment; permit id provides traceability to specific decisions whose evidence is referenced.
Unique permit identifier supports incident reconstruction; not enough on its own.
Tenancy boundary identifier supports demonstrating logical access controls between tenants.

For ADMT used in significant decisions per §7150(b)(3), the risk assessment must identify the output of the ADMT and how the business will use the output to make a significant decision. The permit's decision field IS that output.
Article 12 logging requires recordkeeping of AI system events; the decision is the central event.

The Permit decision is the pre-dispatch authorization outcome for a tool call: allow / deny / throttle / challenge, recorded before managed provider dispatch, with only allow authorizing execution. Control title verified verbatim 2026-08-13.

Maps to the pre-execution hook / policy-engine component of B006.3 only. The sandbox and container configuration, filesystem and network restriction, and tool-definition integrity components are out of Permit scope. Control title verified verbatim 2026-08-13.
Provides human-readable narrative supporting the documentation of ADMT logic; structured decision_details is the more rigorous evidence.
The decision_details code + reason captures the ADMT's logic at evaluation time, including assumptions/limitations expressed as policy rules.
Documents the actions the ADMT system takes based on the decision output.
Supports verification of consumer requests; subject identifier is the binding from a permit to a verifiable consumer.
Identifies the subject for access-control audit purposes.
Action name supports identifying the purpose for processing; full purpose documentation is broader and lives in policy_id/policy_version.
action_name identifies the specific operation being authorized, which is what tool-call validation and authorization is applied against. Pairs with customer-owned review of tool-usage patterns.
Identifies the third party (AI provider) to whom the business discloses or makes available consumers' personal information for processing.
Deployer obligation to use AI systems as instructed; identifying the specific provider/model is necessary to match against the provider's instructions.
Supports identifying the scale of processing (approximate consumer count and per-decision data volume).
Cryptographic fingerprint of stable request semantics enables tamper-detection and replay verification.
Automatic logging of AI events; fingerprint is part of the event record.
Cryptographic binding of the dispatched request to the permit decision supports policies/procedures ensuring ADMT works as intended (i.e., no covert request alteration).
Evidence that the request as evaluated matches the request as dispatched is foundational to event integrity in the logging requirement.
Idempotency keys support deduplication and replay-safety of automated operations.

Policy version stamp identifies the specific policies/procedures the business has implemented to ensure ADMT works as intended; combined with policy diff tracking, supports change-management evidence.
Policy version on every decision enables traceability to a specific change-management record.
policy_id + policy_version identify the exact policy-engine configuration in force at decision time, supporting the pre-execution policy-engine configuration evidence B006.3 describes.
Timestamp drives retention-period calculation; risk assessment must document retention period and criteria. Combined with retention engine, supports the §7155 timing requirements.

Article 26(6) requires high-risk AI deployer logs to be retained for an adequate period determined by applicable law and counsel review; created_at is the anchor for whatever retention window the customer applies.
Permit timestamp supports the retention defense under deletion-exception carve-outs (security/integrity per (d)(2); legal-obligation retention per (d)(8)).
Lineage supports documenting the business's planned method for collecting/using/disclosing personal information across multi-step automated workflows.
Lifecycle status (evaluated, bound, dispatched, closed, expired, revoked) supports tracing incident scope to specific permit lifecycle stages.

controls.rationale: Independent third-party time witness on integrity checkpoints supports the change-detection / file-integrity-monitoring point of focus under CC7.2 ('Implements Change-Detection Mechanisms — The IT system includes a change-detection mechanism, for example, file integrity monitoring tools, to alert personnel to unauthorized modifications'). RFC 3161 timestamps bind the chain state to an externally witnessed time, which is one form of integrity monitoring evidence.
controls.correction_note: Earlier draft labeled this CC7.5 (Logging). That was a mislabel: CC7.5 verbatim is 'The entity identifies, develops, and implements activities to recover from identified security incidents' — recovery, not logging. TSC has no standalone 'Logging' criterion; logging-related evidence lives under CC2.1 (information quality), CC4.1 (ongoing monitoring), and CC7.2 (change-detection). Corrected 2026-05-10 against the authoritative AICPA publication.

nist_ai_rmf.verbatim: AI system security and resilience — as identified in the MAP function — are evaluated and documented.

nist_ai_rmf.verbatim: Risks associated with transparency and accountability — as identified in the MAP function — are examined and documented.

nist_ai_rmf.verbatim: The AI model is explained, validated, and documented, and AI system output is interpreted within its context — as identified in the MAP function — to inform responsible use and governance.

mitre_atlas.scope_note: Permit is pre-execution authorization plus tamper-evident post-execution evidence — NOT an EDR/SOC tool, NOT adversary detection. Mappings below are limited to techniques where the Permit primitive directly authorizes/denies the action OR the audit chain provides authoritative evidence of what was authorized vs attempted vs executed. Recon/Discovery/Lateral-Movement tactics are out of scope.

technique_mappings.permit_evidence: Permit primitive IS the pre-execution authorization for inference API access. Every call produces a decision artifact (allow/deny/challenge) bound to subject_id, resource_provider, and resource_model. Audit chain provides post-hoc evidence of every authorized inference.

Permit policy_id can encode allowlist of approved model surfaces; resource_provider + resource_model identify the specific model boundary on every decision. Permit alone does not control credentials or infrastructure access — necessary but not enough on its own.
Permit logs every authorized invocation of the AI-enabled service. Does not prevent abuse via the legitimate product surface, but provides forensic evidence of usage patterns.

Permit audit chain provides tamper-evident record of which actions were authorized vs denied. Does NOT prevent application-layer exploits; provides post-incident forensic evidence about what the attacker was authorized to do post-exploit.

Permit gates action_name and actions_json — agents can only invoke commands/scripts the policy authorizes. Permit lineage (parent_permit_id) tracks compositional script execution. Denied permits log attempted unauthorized invocations.

binding_request_hash binds the canonical wire body at dispatch — post-decision request alteration (one class of prompt injection) is cryptographically detectable. Does not prevent prompt-injection at the input layer; provides evidence chain of what was authorized vs what was dispatched.

Every agent tool invocation requires a Permit. action_name identifies the tool; actions_json captures parameters; subject_id binds the invoking agent. Constraints/budgets prevent escalation via legitimate tools.

technique_mappings.tactic: AML.TA0007 Defense Evasion / AML.TA0012 Privilege Escalation
technique_mappings.permit_evidence: Even if a model is jailbroken, the Permit policy gates which actions can be invoked downstream — jailbreaking the model does not bypass policy enforcement on resulting tool calls. Audit chain records denied permits showing jailbreak-induced unauthorized requests.

Permit budgets_json caps per-window token/cost consumption — limits bulk-exfiltration via inference. estimated_output_tokens + actual_output_tokens enable detection of unusual extraction volume. closure record's provider_response_digest_v1 binds what was actually returned for post-incident forensics.

binding_request_hash detects if the system prompt portion of the request was altered post-decision. closure record bundles the actual output bytes — supports post-hoc detection of system-prompt leakage in responses.

Permit budgets_json enforces per-subject rate and cost limits at pre-execution — directly prevents cost-based and request-volume DoS. Quota envelope denies further calls when limits are hit, with full denial audit trail.

budgets_json is the direct control for cost harvesting. usage_ledger reconciles authorized vs actual cost; denied permits log attempted budget overruns. Replay enables forensic attribution of cost-harvesting attempts.

technique_mappings.technique_name: Spamming AI System with Chaff Data
technique_mappings.permit_evidence: Permit budgets + rate limits restrict chaff-data injection volume. Does not detect chaff quality; provides bound on chaff quantity.

owasp_api_top_10_2023.scope_note: Permit primitive is API-level governance. Natural mappings concentrate on authorization (API1, API3, API5), resource consumption (API4, API6), and AI-provider consumption (API10). Permit provides necessary identity binding for API2. Permit does NOT address SSRF (API7) or system-configuration (API8); those are explicit non-mappings.

item_mappings.name: Broken Object Level Authorization
item_mappings.permit_evidence: Permit binds subject_id + project_id + resource (resource_provider + resource_model) to every authorized action. Does NOT replace per-object authorization in the application layer, but provides tamper-evident decision evidence at the AI-action boundary.

item_mappings.name: Broken Authentication
item_mappings.permit_evidence: Permit framework requires authenticated identity (subject_id) on every decision — broken authentication upstream propagates into broken Permit evidence. Audit chain provides forensic record of which authenticated principal performed each action.

item_mappings.name: Broken Object Property Level Authorization
item_mappings.permit_evidence: Permit decision_details + constraints_json can encode property-level access rules (e.g., redaction policies). Closure record's client_response_digest_v1 binds the actual bytes delivered for post-hoc property-level audit.

item_mappings.name: Unrestricted Resource Consumption
item_mappings.permit_evidence: Permit budgets_json enforces per-subject, per-project, and per-window consumption limits at pre-execution. usage_ledger reconciles authorized vs actual; denials log attempted overruns. This is the direct mapping — Permit is purpose-built for AI resource consumption governance.

item_mappings.name: Broken Function Level Authorization
item_mappings.permit_evidence: Permit action_name + policy_id gate which functions/actions a subject can invoke. Every authorized function call produces an audit record; denials log attempted unauthorized invocations.

item_mappings.name: Unrestricted Access to Sensitive Business Flows
item_mappings.permit_evidence: Permit policy can encode business-flow-level constraints (e.g., per-flow budgets, per-flow subject restrictions). policy_id stamps the flow that authorized the action. Necessary for flow-level governance; direct support only when paired with business-flow policy authoring.

item_mappings.name: Improper Inventory Management
item_mappings.permit_evidence: resource_provider + resource_model + project_id on every Permit forms a queryable inventory of which AI APIs were used by which projects. Signed audit exports retain this inventory tamper-evidently. Does not catch unused/legacy APIs that never produce Permits.

item_mappings.name: Unsafe Consumption of APIs
item_mappings.permit_evidence: Permit governs outbound AI provider API consumption: resource_provider + resource_model identify the third party, closure record's provider_response_digest_v1 binds what was actually returned, allowing detection of unsafe responses post-hoc.

fedramp.scope_note: Evidence-support mapping for selected NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 controls inside a customer's own authorization boundary. Coverage is strongest in AU audit-and-accountability controls, with partial support in selected AC, CM, CA, IR, SI, and SC controls.
fedramp.baseline_applicability_note: FedRAMP baselines select different NIST SP 800-53 controls. Customers should consult their selected baseline workbook to determine applicability.

control_mappings.permit_evidence: Every Permit decision is an event log entry. Per-project hash chain makes captured event continuity verifiable. resource_provider + resource_model + action_name + subject_id form the event description. Permit substrate captures governed AI-decision events emitted by Keel and supports AU-2 evidence at the AI-action boundary.
Permit decision and closure fields record event type, time, resource, subject, outcome, policy version, and execution context for governed AI actions.
Permit evidence should be paired with customer-defined storage-capacity and retention controls. Signed exports support customer archive workflows.

control_mappings.control_title: Audit Record Review, Analysis, and Reporting
control_mappings.permit_evidence: Signed audit export bundles and verifier output support customer review, analysis, and reporting workflows for governed AI actions.

control_mappings.control_title: Audit Record Reduction and Report Generation
control_mappings.permit_evidence: Audit export bundle is queryable and content-addressed via manifest. Customer integrates Keel exports with their reporting workflows. Permit substrate provides the records; reduction/report generation lives in the customer's reporting layer.
Permit timestamps and RFC 3161 timestamp receipts, when present, support independent time evidence for integrity checkpoints.

Per-project hash chain detects unauthorized modification of covered audit records because each record is cryptographically bound to its predecessor via SHA-256. Ed25519 signed exports detect post-export modification. These primitives support AU-9 audit-information integrity evidence; customer access-control design remains separate.

control_mappings.control_title: Protection of Audit Information | Store on Separate Physical Systems or Components
control_mappings.permit_evidence: External checkpoint anchoring can store signed chain snapshots separately from primary audit storage.

control_mappings.control_title: Protection of Audit Information | Cryptographic Protection
control_mappings.permit_evidence: Hash chain (SHA-256), Ed25519 signed exports, RFC 3161 TSA receipts. Three cryptographic protection mechanisms are layered: chain integrity, export authenticity, and time-witnessing. These named, auditable primitives support AU-9(3) cryptographic-integrity evidence.
Ed25519 signed exports, public key manifests, and timestamp receipts support scoped signature-attribution evidence for exported AI-action records.
Signed exports can be archived to support customer-defined audit-retention requirements. Retention duration remains a customer control and contract question.

The Permit primitive generates AI-action audit records for governed requests. Hash-chain continuity makes covered record deletion or reordering detectable. Every governed Permit produces a record; bypassed traffic outside Keel is out of scope.

Permit is the AI-action access enforcement mechanism. policy_id + policy_version stamp the enforcement rule; subject_id binds the requesting identity. Denied permits log unauthorized-access attempts. Note: AC-3 covers system access broadly; Permit enforces at the AI-action boundary only — system-level access enforcement remains customer responsibility.

Policies can encode least-privilege rules for AI actions (e.g., agent X may invoke only tool subset Y). Permit denials evidence least-privilege enforcement. Customer is responsible for authoring least-privilege policies; Permit enforces and evidences them.
policy_id and policy_version fields bind each AI decision to a specific policy configuration version and support customer change-traceability evidence.

resource_provider + resource_model on every Permit forms a queryable inventory of AI components used (which providers, which models). Supports the AI portion of system component inventory. Customer responsible for general system component inventory beyond AI components.

Per-project hash chain emits continuous audit evidence. External checkpoint cadence (every 5 minutes) provides ongoing integrity proof. Replay drift detection identifies behavioral changes over time. Provides the AI-action telemetry for the customer's continuous monitoring program.

Incident evidence export bundle (shipped 2026-04-25) packages signed evidence for incident response workflows. Tampering detection codes (WALK_RECORD_HASH_MISMATCH, WALK_CLOSURE_DISPATCH_DIGEST_MISMATCH, etc.) provide specific incident classification for AI-integrity events. Supports customer IR program for AI-related incidents; does not provide general incident response.

Replay drift detection is the AI-incident monitoring surface — identifies emerging decision drift, policy violations, and integrity events. Customer integrates with their SIEM for cross-surface incident monitoring.

Hash chain integrity + Ed25519 signed exports + RFC 3161 timestamps provide cryptographic integrity evidence for AI-decision information. Build SHA stamped on every governance event provides code-level traceability. Verifier CLI checks integrity without vendor access. These artifacts support SI-7 integrity-verification evidence for the Permit substrate.
Signed exports and customer archives can support AI-evidence retention. Customer information-management policies remain outside Permit scope.

Named cryptographic primitives used: SHA-256 (chain), Ed25519 (signatures), AES-256-GCM (provider key encryption), RFC 3161 (timestamping). All NIST-approved or industry-standard primitives. Cryptographic protection is design-level not bolt-on.
Signed exports, hash-chain integrity, and checkpoint evidence protect AI evidence with cryptographic integrity. Customer confidentiality controls remain separate.

uncovered_high_priority_controls.status: OUT OF SCOPE FOR PERMIT SUBSTRATE

requirement_mappings.name: Support information security with organizational policies and programs
requirement_mappings.permit_evidence: Permit policy artifacts and policy versions can support AI-governance policy evidence. Organization-wide security policy remains customer-owned.

out_of_scope_requirements: Requirement 1 Install and maintain network security controls — customer network responsibility
Requirement 2 Apply secure configurations to all system components — customer config baseline responsibility
Requirement 3 Protect stored account data — Permit substrate doesn't touch cardholder data
Requirement 4 Protect cardholder data with strong cryptography during transmission over open, public networks — TLS/transport layer responsibility outside Permit substrate
Requirement 5 Protect all systems and networks from malicious software — customer EDR/anti-malware responsibility
Requirement 8 Identify users and authenticate access to system components — customer IAM responsibility
Requirement 9 Restrict physical access to cardholder data — physical security responsibility
Requirement 11 Test security of systems and networks regularly — customer vulnerability scanning / pentesting responsibility
pci_dss.broad_scoping_caveat: PCI DSS applies to entities that handle cardholder data within a Cardholder Data Environment. These mappings are for customer AI workloads that are inside that scope.

owasp_asvs.version_note: ASVS v5.0.0 chapter numbering differs from v4; cite the v5 version qualifier when using these mappings.

chapter_mappings.permit_evidence: Permit primitive is API governance: every AI API call requires a decision, with subject + resource + action attribution. Signed exports + closure records provide tamper-evident API-call evidence. Use as primary chapter for ASVS-aligned coverage claims.

Permit IS the AI-action authorization layer. policy_id + policy_version stamp the authorization rule; subject_id + resource binding produces the decision record. Denied permits log unauthorized-attempt evidence.
Hash-chain integrity, Ed25519 signed exports, timestamp receipts, externally anchored checkpoints, and key manifests provide cryptographic integrity evidence.
policy_id and policy_version provide AI-governance configuration traceability. Runtime and infrastructure configuration remain outside Permit scope.
Permit closure records and signed exports protect AI evidence with cryptographic integrity. General data-protection compliance remains customer-owned.

chapter_mappings.chapter: V16 Security Logging and Error Handling
chapter_mappings.permit_evidence: Per-project hash chain + Ed25519 signatures + RFC 3161 timestamps provide tamper-evident security logging for the AI surface. Tampering-detection codes (WALK_RECORD_HASH_MISMATCH, etc.) provide specific error classification. Independent verifier CLI enables verification without vendor account.

aiuc_1_q3_2026.scope_note: Evidence-support mapping for selected AIUC-1 controls, pinned to the Q3-2026 edition. AIUC-1 certification is per-agent and is granted by an accredited auditor; the applicable control set is fixed in an auditor-signed Statement of Applicability. Nothing here is a certification claim. Reverify each quarter.
aiuc_1_q3_2026.verification_note: A008.3, B006.3, D003, and D004 control titles were verified verbatim on 2026-08-13. The E015 series is corroborated only — see the per-control verification field.

control_mappings.permit_evidence: In managed-execution mode the calling agent holds only a Keel credential; downstream provider credentials are custodied by Keel and retrieved at point of use, so the agent never holds them. This supports the per-tool and per-session scoping and just-in-time retrieval expectations. Secret management for the customer's own systems remains customer-owned.

explicit_non_mappings.rationale: This trigger was not included in the final adopted text. Final scope is limited to ADMT used to replace human decisionmaking for significant decisions, or training ADMT for those uses or for identity/biological profiling technology.
This sub-block was not included in final §7152(a)(2); final text requires a concise explanation of assessment purpose.
The detailed proposed evaluation framework was reduced in the final adopted text to policy, procedure, and training requirements.

SSRF is a transport-layer/application-layer concern handled by network egress controls, URL allowlists, and request-validation libraries in the application. Permit primitive operates at the AI decision boundary and does not control outbound HTTP behavior at the network layer. Customers should address API7 via standard application-security controls.

Security Misconfiguration spans deployment configuration, framework defaults, HTTP headers, error verbosity, and infrastructure hardening — none of which the Permit primitive addresses. Customers should address API8 via standard application-security configuration baselines (e.g., CIS benchmarks).
ASVS v5.0.0 V17 covers WebRTC peer-connection security. Permit primitive is HTTP-API governance and has no WebRTC surface.

Discovery techniques (AML.T0007 Discover AI Artifacts, AML.T0013 Discover AI Model Ontology, etc.) describe adversary recon AFTER access has been obtained. Permit does not detect recon behavior — that is a SOC/EDR responsibility. Permit may provide forensic context post-incident but does not provide preventive or detection evidence for this tactic.
Reconnaissance techniques are pre-engagement adversary behavior outside the Permit primitive's scope. Permit operates inside the customer environment at the AI decision boundary.

explicit_non_mappings.control_id: AML.TA0006 Persistence + AML.TA0015 Lateral Movement + AML.TA0014 Command and Control
explicit_non_mappings.rationale: These tactics describe in-environment adversary behavior (persistence mechanisms, lateral movement, C2 channels). Permit governs the AI decision boundary, not host/network telemetry. Mappings to these tactics would be over-claim.
Keel is not a FedRAMP-authorized Cloud Service Offering. This artifact maps Permit evidence to selected customer-side NIST SP 800-53 evidence needs only.

explicit_non_mappings.control_id: Most NIST 800-53 control families outside AU/AC/CM/CA/IR/SI/SC scope (PE, MA, MP, PS, PL, PM, AT, etc.)
explicit_non_mappings.status: OUT OF SCOPE FOR PERMIT SUBSTRATE
explicit_non_mappings.rationale: NIST 800-53 Rev 5 contains 20 control families and 1000+ controls/enhancements. The Permit substrate naturally maps to subsets of 7 families (AU, AC, CM, CA, IR, SI, SC) where AI-decision evidence is load-bearing. The other 13 families (Physical & Environmental Protection PE, Maintenance MA, Media Protection MP, Personnel Security PS, Planning PL, Program Management PM, Awareness and Training AT, etc.) are entirely customer responsibility and unrelated to AI-decision substrate. Listing them as 'mapped' would be over-claim.

explicit_non_mappings.control_id: AU-9(4) Protection of Audit Information | Access by Subset of Privileged Users
explicit_non_mappings.rationale: Cryptographic integrity (any tampering is detectable post-hoc) is different from access-control on READING audit logs. Keel substrate provides integrity; customer-side IAM/RBAC determines who can read audit exports. Customers should not claim AU-9(4) compliance based on Keel substrate alone.
Keel is not a PCI DSS validated service provider. This artifact maps Permit evidence to selected customer-side evidence needs only when the customer workload is in PCI DSS scope.

explicit_non_mappings.control_id: PCI DSS broadly when AI workloads do NOT touch CDE
explicit_non_mappings.status: OUT OF SCOPE WHEN NO CDE TOUCHPOINT EXISTS
explicit_non_mappings.rationale: PCI DSS does not apply to AI workloads that do not process payment card data within a Cardholder Data Environment. These mappings are for the narrower in-scope case.

explicit_non_mappings.status: OUT OF SCOPE FOR PERMIT SUBSTRATE
explicit_non_mappings.rationale: Of the 18 CIS Controls v8.1, 12 are entirely outside Permit substrate scope (asset inventory, software inventory, account management, vulnerability management, email/browser, malware defense, data recovery, network management, network monitoring, training, penetration testing). Permit substrate covers ~6 of 18 with varying strength; CIS Control 8 (Audit Log Management) is the only direct-support fit; Controls 3, 4, 6, 15, 16, 17 have partial alignment.

Keel is not AIUC-1 certified and does not make an agent AIUC-1 compliant. Certification is per-agent, scoped through an auditor-signed Statement of Applicability, and granted by an accredited auditor. This artifact maps Permit evidence to selected customer-side AIUC-1 evidence needs only.

D004 requires appointing qualified third-party assessors and performing assessments of tool calls at least every quarter. Keel's own conformance tests do not satisfy it, and this is distinct from AIUC's separate re-run of its technical evaluations at re-certification. Control title and the assessor and quarterly language verified verbatim 2026-08-13.

explicit_non_mappings.control_id: B006.3 sandbox, container, filesystem, network, and tool-definition-integrity components
explicit_non_mappings.status: OUT OF SCOPE FOR PERMIT SUBSTRATE
explicit_non_mappings.rationale: Permit evidence covers the pre-execution hook / policy-engine component of B006.3 only. Sandbox and container configuration, filesystem and network restriction for agent code execution environments, and detection of unauthorized post-approval tool-definition changes are customer-owned.

explicit_non_mappings.status: OUT OF SCOPE FOR PERMIT SUBSTRATE
explicit_non_mappings.rationale: Keel is not a content-safety or model-evaluation platform. Permit evidence records the authorization decision and its enforcement, not the safety of model output.

explicit_non_mappings.control_id: B010 (secure code generation) and generated-code vulnerability controls
explicit_non_mappings.status: OUT OF SCOPE FOR PERMIT SUBSTRATE
explicit_non_mappings.rationale: B010 was added as a new mandatory requirement in the Q3-2026 update and concerns vulnerability prevention in generated code. Permit evidence does not analyze generated code.
Red-teaming, including the interim quarterly red-teaming AIUC-1 expects, is performed by the customer and its assessors. Permit evidence is not a substitute for adversarial testing.
